Royal Law
ROY-ul LAW
n. phrase (from James 2:8; the summary command “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” as the law of the King)
Royal from Latin regalis (kingly, regal), from rex (king); law from Old English lagu (that which is laid down, fixed). The phrase “royal law” appears explicitly in James 2:8, where the apostle calls Leviticus 19:18 — “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” — the nomos basilikos (kingly/royal law). The law is “royal” because it is the law of the King of kings, because it is the summary command of the supreme lawgiver, and because it governs the kingdom citizens.

Biblical Definition

The royal law (James 2:8) is the apostle's citation of Leviticus 19:18 — “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” — identified as the nomos basilikos, the law belonging to the King. James invokes it in the context of rebuking partiality: showing deference to the rich while dishonoring the poor violates the royal law because love of neighbor makes no such distinction. The background is Jesus' own identification of Leviticus 19:18 as the second great commandment, together with love of God, summing up the whole Law and the Prophets (Matthew 22:37–40). Paul similarly identifies neighbor-love as the fulfillment of the law (Romans 13:9; Galatians 5:14). For James, calling this command “royal” carries a threefold weight: it is the King's own law (Christ the King has ratified it); it is the crown law of the kingdom (the law that governs how citizens of the kingdom treat one another); and it is the law that judges the judge (James goes on to warn that the same law that commands love also warns of judgment for partial love). The royal law therefore functions as both the positive summary of Christian social ethics and a judicial standard: to profess the faith of the King while practicing favoritism is to break the King's own law. James 2:10 presses the point: whoever stumbles at one point is guilty of all — partial obedience to a royal command is still disobedience.

Webster 1828 Definition

The “royal law” of James 2:8 — “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18) — the King's own summary of social ethics in the kingdom; the law that governs relationships among kingdom citizens and judges partial or preferential love as lawbreaking.

ROYAL LAW, n. [Latin regalis, kingly.] The law of the King; specifically, the command of James 2:8 citing Leviticus 19:18: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Called “royal” because it belongs to the King of kings, because it is the summary law of His kingdom, and because it governs the social ethics of all kingdom citizens.

James employs the phrase in the context of rebuking economic partiality in worship: showing preferential honor to the rich man while dishonoring the poor man violates the royal law because neighbor-love admits no social distinction. The church pew is not organized by wealth; the King's law governs alike every kingdom citizen.

Jesus' citation of Leviticus 19:18 as the second great commandment (Matthew 22:39) and Paul's citation of it as the fulfillment of the law (Romans 13:9; Galatians 5:14) establish the royal law's canonical centrality. James' terminology adds the royal dimension: this is not merely a summary of social ethics but the explicit law of the King who is both lawgiver and judge.

The “royal” designation also signals that the law's authority exceeds social contract or common moral instinct. It is not derived from the Golden Rule as a human rationalization but proceeds from the King who declares what His subjects owe one another. The church does not negotiate or moderate the command; she receives it from the King.

James 2:10–11 presses the judicial implication: the one who keeps the whole law yet stumbles in one point is guilty of all, for the same God who commanded neighbor-love also commanded the other precepts. Selective obedience to a royal law is still treason — James does not allow a partial-obedience escape.

Key Scripture

James 2:8 — "If ye fulfil the royal law according to the scripture, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, ye do well:"

James 2:10 — "For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all."

Leviticus 19:18 — "Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD."

Matthew 22:39 — "And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself."

Modern Corruption

The social-justice movement has detached “love your neighbor” from its royal source and its judicial weight, reducing it to a progressive political framework that redefines “neighbor” as political class and “love” as advocacy for redistribution rather than covenantal service.

expand to see more

Progressive social-justice theology has appropriated James' “royal law” as a mandate for structural political action — defining “neighbor” as an oppressed identity class and “loving your neighbor” as advocating for redistributive policy and challenging systemic inequality. This reading detaches the command from its royal source (the King who defines both neighbor and love) and from its judicial weight (James' warning that partial love is lawbreaking). The royal law is not a political program; it is a personal command that governs how every kingdom citizen treats every other person, regardless of social category.

A second corruption strips the command of its covenantal particularity by reading it as the universal Golden Rule: a rational human instinct dressed in biblical language. This makes Leviticus 19:18 redundant to Confucius or Kant and loses the phrase's royal weight. James calls it the law of the King because it is the King's command, backed by the King's judgment (2:12–13). The neighbor-love command is not rationally derivable without the King; it is received from the King and practiced before His face.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The royal law flows from Leviticus 19:18 in the Holiness Code, is ratified by Jesus as the second great commandment, is cited by Paul as the fulfillment of the law, and is named “royal” by James — the full canonical weight of neighbor-love from Sinai to the New Testament letters.

expand to see more

Leviticus 19:18 (Holiness Code) — “You shall love your neighbor as yourself: I am the LORD”; the divine self-declaration at the end of the command grounds it in covenantal identity, not social contract; love of neighbor is owed because the LORD commands it.

Matthew 22:37–40 (Two Great Commandments) — Jesus pairs Deuteronomy 6:5 (love of God) with Leviticus 19:18 (love of neighbor) as the double hinge on which the whole Law and Prophets hang; no other commandment stands apart from these two.

Romans 13:9 and Galatians 5:14 — Paul cites Leviticus 19:18 as the single-sentence fulfillment of the second table of the Decalogue; all specific social commands are applications of neighbor-love.

James 2:8–13 (royal law and judgment) — James not only names the command “royal” but immediately presses its judicial consequence: partial love of the rich while dishonoring the poor breaks the royal law, and the same law-giver who commanded love will judge the partial liver.

Luke 10:25–37 (Good Samaritan) — Jesus' parable in response to “Who is my neighbor?” redefines the neighbor from ethnic category to any person one encounters in need, extending Leviticus 19:18 beyond Israel's borders while keeping its concrete, embodied character.

Usage

"The royal law's judicial weight is its corrective to sentimental interpretations of neighbor-love: James does not say “try to love your neighbor” but “fulfill the royal law” and warns immediately that failing at one point makes a person guilty of all — it is the King's law, not an aspiration."

"The command to love your neighbor “as yourself” assumes proper self-knowledge, not self-love as modern psychology defines it: one who does not properly regard his own embodied, image-bearing dignity cannot properly regard his neighbor's; the command assumes a realistic anthropology, not therapeutic self-affirmation."

"Pastors preaching the royal law must hold together James' two emphases: the positive command (love your neighbor, make no social distinction in the assembly) and the judicial warning (the same King who commanded love will judge partial obedience) — neighbor-love is not optional encouragement but royal statute."
